To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

nickel(II) ions, in the presence of hydrogen peroxide, can cause damage to the bases of the DNA in chromosomal DNA isolated from cells of human origin and that this damage is similar to that caused by the hydroxyl free radical.
nickel and cobalt, two metal ions that are carcinogenic to humans, can damage DNA in chromatin by generating hydroxyl radical in the presence of hydrogen peroxide.
Ni(II) ions, in the presence of hydrogen peroxide, produce chemical changes in DNA in human cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of the carcinogenesis of nickel(II) and cobalt( II) compounds.
the chemical and biological properties of nickel and cobalt compounds and how these compounds cause cancer in laboratory animals and in humans.
the mechanisms of metal-induced DNA damage and the possible role of metal ions in cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Ni(II)-dependent and Co(II)-dependent formation of DNA base damage in chromatin by H2O2 is due to a "site-specific" production of hydroxyl radicals from unchelated metal ions bound to the chromatin.
Ni(II) is a genotoxin in chromatin and a possible human carcinogen.

Ni(II) ions, in the presence of a source of H2O 2, cause DNA base damage to the bases of DNA in chromatin, and that Co(II) does the same, although the latter is a weaker inducer of base damage than the former.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ni(II) ions are more efficient than Co(II) in producing base damage in chromatin in the presence of hydrogen peroxide.
nickel(II) ions, but not cobalt(II) ions or iron(II) ions (which were used as controls), in the presence of hydrogen peroxide caused damage to DNA bases in human chromatin.
Ni(II) is more genotoxic to human cells than Co(II) and that both Ni(II) (and Co(II)) ions are more genotoxic to the DNA of chromatin than to DNA alone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ni(II) ions are able to produce DNA base damage in human chromatin, and this damage is enhanced when H2O2 is present.
the DNA in chroma tin is much more susceptible to damage by Ni(II)/O2- or Co(II)/O-2 than is DNA isolated from chromatin.
the Ni(II) ion in the presence of hydrogen peroxide is a potent inducer of oxidative DNA damage in chromosomal DNA.
